item.title: The Economy Is Less K-Shaped than You Think
item.content:encoded:
October 31, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

The first chart below shows that nominal spending growth has been broadly similar across income groups since 2024, all running at roughly 4-5% YoY.

The second chart shows that household net worth has risen substantially across the income distribution since 2019, including by around 80% for the bottom 20%.

item.title: The Search for Duration Leads to Credit
item.content:encoded:
October 30, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Treasury issuance in 2026 has a weighted average maturity of just 1.7 years. For US corporate bonds, it’s almost 10 years, see chart below.

One reason companies are issuing long is the scale of today’s buildout in long-duration assets like data centers, power generation, grid infrastructure and manufacturing facilities, which are financed over the long term, not quarter to quarter. For investors with obligations that stretch out for decades, like insurers and pension funds, the search for duration leads naturally to different types of credit.

The bottom line is that when the government issues short and companies issue long, the investors who need duration most will go where the duration is.

item.title: What Makes a Moat?
item.content:encoded:
October 29, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

With AI disruption potentially around the corner, there is a lot of discussion about moats at the moment.

Professor Aswath Damodaran’s framework looks at the sources of competitive advantage: brand strength, switching costs, network effects, cost advantages and legal protection, see chart below.

The key distinction is not simply whether a company has a moat, but how wide and durable that moat is, and how it shows up in the numbers: pricing power, customer retention, market share and profitability.

For investors, understanding the source and sustainability of a company’s competitive advantage is critical to assessing its long-term value.

With the proliferation of AI, the moat discussion is becoming even more important. Here is a simple checklist of three questions to ask.

The AI moat checklist: Data, Workflow, Pricing

  1. Data: Does the company own data its rivals can’t get?
  2. Workflow: Is the company’s product part of how customers do their jobs every day?
  3. Pricing power: Can the company charge more without customers walking away?

item.title: A Future Congress Will Have to Fix Social Security
item.content:encoded:
October 28, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Social Security is financed mainly by a 12.4% payroll tax on wages up to an annual cap, split between workers and employers, with additional revenue from income taxes on benefits and interest on trust fund reserves.

Since costs now exceed income, the retirement trust fund is being drawn down and is projected to be depleted in late 2032, according to the 2026 Trustees Report, see chart below.

Once reserves run out, the program can pay only what it takes in, about 78% of scheduled benefits, a cut of roughly 22% unless Congress acts. Combining the retirement and disability funds, which would require legislation, would delay depletion to 2034, with about 83% of benefits payable.

Closing the gap would require raising revenue (a higher payroll tax rate or taxable wage cap), reducing benefits (a later retirement age or slower cost-of-living adjustments) or a combination of both.

The bottom line is that a possible 22% benefit cut makes it more important for households to save more and build a stream of income in retirement.

item.title: The Inflation Debate Is No Longer Just About Supply
item.content:encoded:
October 27, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Data from the San Francisco Fed shows that core PCE inflation at 3% is split evenly between supply and demand, see chart below.

In 2022, supply was the largest driver.

The rise in the demand contribution since 2024 suggests inflation is no longer just a supply story. That matters for the Fed, because interest rates can cool demand-driven inflation but do little about supply shocks.

item.title: Rents Face Renewed Upward Pressure as the Housing Supply Wave Fades
item.content:encoded:
October 26, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Every housing market has a long-term average for how much new rental housing gets built each year, measured as a percentage of its existing stock. For example, a metro might typically add about 2% to its apartment inventory annually. During the construction boom, many markets ran well above their own average, creating the “supply wave” that held down rents.

The equilibrium date is the point where a market’s new supply rate falls back to its own long-term average. Before that date, supply is above normal and can hold down rents. After it, supply is at or below normal, so that puts upward pressure on rents.

The chart below shows that only Tampa, Philadelphia and Austin are still forecasted to have above-average rental supply. With new buildings taking 12-18 months to lease up, the fading supply wave is set to put upward pressure on rents and, by extension, on shelter inflation into 2027. This complicates the Fed’s task, with inflation already running above its 2% target.

For more discussion, see our Daily Spark on the higher rates, higher rent doom loop.

item.title: Japan Weeks Preview: Activism Meets Rising Profits
item.content:encoded:
October 25, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Japan Weeks (Oct. 26-30), now in its fourth year, brings global investors and asset managers together to explore the opportunities in Japan’s financial and capital markets. One of the most important themes behind that opportunity is shareholder activism, which is reshaping corporate Japan. Shareholder proposals have more than tripled since 2018, reflecting a stronger focus on governance and shareholder value, see first chart below. This is starting to translate into stronger corporate profits, with profits at Japan’s medium-sized businesses (those with capital of JPY 100 million to 1 billion) reaching historically high levels, a sign that improving profitability extends well beyond the country’s largest companies, see second and third charts.

item.title: No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector
item.content:encoded:
October 24, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech. Revenue per worker is rising for the Mag 7 but is flat for the S&P 493, see the first chart below. Profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but are flat for the S&P 493, see the second chart below. And there are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth, see the third chart below. With no impact on the bottom line, mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.

VC-backed companies are spending more and more on tokens, but mainstream corporate America does not need the latest model and is unwilling to pay for it. As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited, see the fourth and fifth charts below.

The question looking ahead is whether, even as models become commoditized, mainstream corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins. That may be harder than it sounds. AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment. Judgment depends on context, and the answer varies with which human or which model you ask. Perhaps most importantly, AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.

The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.

item.title: Circularity in AI Shows Up in Token Spending Too
item.content:encoded:
October 22, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Ramp data show that 80% of the top 1% of AI spenders are VC-backed, compared with only 13% of the median spender, suggesting that the circularity seen among AI hyperscalers and model providers also extends to token spending, as the startups buying the most compute are paying for it with venture capital rather than organic earnings, see chart below.

If the AI payoff is slow to materialize or never arrives, VC returns would come under pressure, since the capital funding today’s token spending would have little to show for it, and a pullback in venture funding could in turn weaken demand for compute.
